en: Having combined the two texts on the ritual procedures for the twelve devas into a single manual, the *Homa-vidhi* (Ritual of Fire Offering) is set forth:
one should spread *kuśa* grass, or lotus leaves, or other green grass, upon the eight directions of the practice site.
Alternatively, having smeared a circular altar, one establishes ten positions. To the left and right of Śakra, one places Brahmā and Bhauma.
The positions,
together with the eight directions, total ten.
If there is no place within the site of enlightenment (maṇḍala) to establish these positions, [one should proceed accordingly].
Immediately before the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), one should use a pure location to demarcate a separate square boundary.
Within it, the eight directions are laid out,
with two positions established at the center.
Setting aside the Brahma-heaven and the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
one should offer food to the devas of the ten directions using various kinds of congee.
That is to say: boil husked rice, sesame seeds, and mung beans together until they are perfectly pure;
then place them in a fragrant vessel.
First, place a clean leaf at each seat.
Once the circumambulation is completed, place [the items] upon the leaves.
First, fill a pure vessel with water.
Then, write a small amount of scented water upon a leaf and offer it.
Next, snap the ring finger and middle finger of the right hand over a small amount of unguent.
Then, offer a single flower and place it upon the seat. Finally, offer incense.
Next, burn Brahma-incense.
Offer it before the seats;
use this same single burner for all.
Next, finish one ladle of congee and place it upon the leaf to offer.
Then, take a small wax candle or a paper candle and offer it by inserting it into the congee.
From the scented water to the lamp,
each is consecrated three times with its respective root mantra.
Once the offerings from the water to the lamp have been completed for each individual seat.
However, as for the sequence mentioned above, when offering the attention to the lamps to the various positions,
do not allow them to be extinguished until they have been offered to all.
One must have assistants or several servants,
each holding an object to provide for the task;
if one takes [the lamp] alone, the candle will certainly not last until the work is finished.
Append the words of the specific aspiration sought above each *svāhā*. To the east, Śakra rides upon the white elephant king and dwells amidst clouds of five colors;
his body is golden in hue.
The right hand holds a trident at the heart;
the left hand rests upon the left hip;
the left foot hangs down.
The three goddesses each hold a lotus flower;
some hold various flowers and the like in a tray,
while others hold blue lotuses in a tray.
Regarding the mudrā: the right hand forms a fist and rests at the waist;
the five fingers of the left hand are held straight up and touching one another, with the earth and water fingers (the ring and middle fingers) bent at their middle joints.
The wind [deity] rests its back against fire;
its middle joints are bent inward.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vāyave svāhā*. In the southeast, the Fire Deity rides a blue sheep.
The body is the color of raw meat, with flames pervading it everywhere.
His two right hands hold a green bamboo staff and a *kundika* (water flask);
his two left hands display the *tarjani* (threatening) mudra and hold a rosary.
Two celestial maidens holding heavenly flowers stood to the left and right of the ascetic seer;
they hung their left feet while stepping with their right feet.
As for the mudrā: the left hand forms a fist and rests at the left hip;
the five fingers of the right hand are held straight up and touching one another, with the thumb bent and tucked into the palm.
The wind bends at its joints,
summoning together with *svāhā*.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ āne svāhā. In the south, Yama rides upon a water buffalo.
His right hand holds a banner topped with a human head, and his left hand is held palm-upward.
He is attended by two celestial maidens,
while two ghost-messengers hold swords and brandish halberds.
Red-black in color, with the right foot hanging down.
As for the mudrā: first join the palms;
bend the middle joints of both hands so that their backs touch one another.
The two *vāyu* fingers are also bent back against each other;
by pressing the middle joints of the *vāyu* fingers with the thumbs, it is completed.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ yamāya svāhā. In the southwest, the Lord of the Rākṣasas rides a white lion;
his body is clad in armor.
The right hand holds a knife held upright;
the left hand’s thumb presses down upon the middle and ring fingers.
It is the color of raw flesh.
Two celestial maidens attend to his left and right;
two rākṣasa demons hold three-pronged spears.
Regarding the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand and place it at the right hip.
With the five fingers of the left hand held upright and touching one another, bend the middle joints of the ring finger and little finger toward the earth and water [sections].
By pressing the tips of the index fingers against the earth and water nails, the seal is completed.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ nairṛtyai svāhā. To the west, Varuṇa dwells within the water, riding upon a tortoise.
Light green in color.
His right hand grasps a sword;
his left hand holds a dragon lasso.
Upon the crown are five dragons;
four celestial maidens hold exquisite flowers.
As for the mudrā, the right hand is as described before.
Clench the left hand into a fist,
leaving the hollow space empty so that it does not enter the palm;
the wind [of the breath] then rises directly upward.
If one slightly bends the middle joints, it is accomplished.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ varuṇāya svāhā. To the northwest is the Wind Deity (Vāyu), riding upon a roe deer amidst the clouds and clad in armor.
The left hand rests upon the hip;
the right hand holds a single-pronged head-axe with a vermilion banner atop the blade.
Two celestial maidens attend him.
As for the mudrā of the yakṣa host: the right hand is as described before;
the five fingers of the left hand are held upright, touching one another.
The earth and water [elements] are formed by bending the middle joints. The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vaye vi svāhā. In the north, Vaiśravaṇa sits upon two ghosts.
His body is clad in armor;
his left palm cradles a stūpa,
and his right hand holds a jewel-topped staff.
The body is golden in color.
Two goddesses hold precious flowers and other offerings.
As for the mudrā: first, join the palms together.
Interlace the ten fingers within;
extend the two *āpas* (index fingers) upright with their tips touching,
and extend the two *vāyus* (middle fingers) upright, slightly bent.
The left empty space enters the right palm,
pressing down upon the left fire-armour.
The right empty space passes over the back of the left empty space and enters the left palm.
Press the right hand upon the fire-element armor.
The two winds and the syllable *ha* summon one another.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vaiśravaṇāya svāhā. To the northeast is the deity Īśāna, formerly called Maheśvara.
He is also called Maheśvara.
He rides upon a yellow,
fat bull and holds in his left hand a kapāla cup filled with blood.
His right hand holds a trident wound;
his flesh is a pale blue color, he has three eyes,
and he is wrathful with two fangs protruding upward.
A skull serves as a necklace;
within the head-crown are two upward-facing crescent moons,
and two celestial maidens hold flowers.
As for the mudrā: the right hand forms a fist and rests on the right hip;
the five fingers of the left hand are held straight up and touching one another, with the second and third fingers (earth and water) bent at their middle joints.
For the three mudrās of Fire, Wind, and Space, they are formed by keeping the fingers slightly apart from one another.
The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām īśānāya svāhā*. As for the mudrā of Brahmā of the upper direction: form a fist with the right hand and place it on the right hip.
The five fingers of the left hand are joined together and held upright, slightly bent,
with their height extending just over the shoulder;
this immediately constitutes the visualization of a lotus flower.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mṛlohamaṇi svāhā. Regarding the mudrā of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivīdevatā) of the lower direction: first, join the palms together.
The four fingers below the wind [element] are interlocked;
the front opening is wide open,
and the two voids each rest against the side of the wind.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vītivaye svāhā. As for the mudrā of the Sun Deity (Sūrya), it is no different from the previous mudrā of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī).
Simply by placing the two heads of emptiness each upon the lower joints of the water [elements], it is accomplished.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Anitiye svāhā. As for the mudrā of the Moon Deity, it is like the mudrā of Brahmā described previously.
However, [the hands] are held with palms facing upward,
within which is the mark of a pure white moon.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ caṇḍāya svāhā*. As for the mudrā of the Seven Planets: first, join the palms with the ten fingers touching one another.
The two winds and the two spaces are utterly opened to one another.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, a-ra-he-śva-ri-ya-pra-pa-ta-re-tu-ti-ra-ma-ye svāhā. Regarding the mudrā of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras): first, join the palms with the fingers hollowed.
The two fire fingers are crossed externally;
the two space fingers are also crossed.
The mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ nakṣatranisūdanaye svāhā. Add two positions within the eight directions.
Heaven and earth face each other above and below;
the luminaries shine with the east and the constellations in the west.
All offerings are presented in unison.
If there is a specific vow,
it may also be performed individually;
this applies within the homa altar as well.
Each [deity] is established by focusing the mind according to its respective direction, and their positions are likewise designated,
and so forth. At the center of the mandala, one places the four-armed Acala,
who is the color of blue flesh.
Form two vajra fists with the index and little fingers each bent into the shape of a hook,
placing them at the two corners of the mouth.
The teeth are like [white] tusks;
the right hand holds a sword held upright, and the left hand holds a lasso.
He sits in the half-lotus posture, with the right leg pressing upon the left.
He sat upon a flat rock;
his majestic radiance and brilliance pervaded his entire body like a mass of fire, and so forth.
Now, a diagram of his position is provided.
As for the establishment of the circular altar and so forth,
these may be prepared as the occasion demands;
one should perform the rites facing north.

Alternatively, one may depict the sequence of the Twelve Devas of the Central Terrace Five Great Vidyārājas, taking the Immovable (Acala) Five Great Vidyārājas as the lords of the Twelve Devas; following this sequence of the Twelve Devas, one may offer to the various devī consorts, and subsequently offer to the renowned local deities of the land.
I sought out the imperial manuscript of the *Dongchao Sengzheng* from Zhijiyuan in Luedong,
had it transcribed, and collated it;
this is the upper woodblock.
This was cited as proof from the *Kikigaki*, the *Sōketsu*, the *Kinpōshū*, and other texts.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Kaidō, a student at Chōkō-ji Temple.
